'''Sir Timothy Augustine Coghlan''' {{post-nominals|country=UK|KCMG|ISO|FRSS|MICE}} (9 June 1856 – 30 April 1926) was an Australian statistician, engineer, economic historian and diplomat. He held the post of [[New South Wales]] government statistician for 19 years, and served various periods as [[Agent-General|Agent-General for New South Wales]] in London from 1905 to his death in 1926.<ref name=ADB>Neville Hicks, '[https://adb.anu.edu.au/biography/coghlan-sir-timothy-augustine-5708 Coghlan, Sir Timothy Augustine (1855–1926)]', ''[[Australian Dictionary of Biography]]'', Volume 8, [[Melbourne University Press|MUP]], 1981, pp 48–51.</ref><ref name=DAB>{{Dictionary of Australian Biography|First=Timothy Augustine|Last=Coghlan|shortlink=0-dict-biogCl-Cu.html#coghlan1}}</ref>

==Early life==
Coghlan was born in [[Sydney]], the second son of Thomas Coghlan of [[Irish Catholic|Irish Roman Catholic]] extraction. He was educated at [[Cleveland Street Intensive English High School|Cleveland Street Public School]] and [[Sydney Grammar School]], and in 1873 joined the public works department, becoming assistant-engineer of harbours and rivers in 1884.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article71103310 |title=The Government Statistician. |newspaper=Australian Town And Country Journal |volume=XXXVIII |issue=979 |location=New South Wales, Australia |date=13 October 1888 |accessdate=16 February 2018 |page=28 |via=National Library of Australia}}</ref>

==Other work==
In December 1905, Coghlan was offered the chance to become the inaugural [[Australian Statistician|Commonwealth Statistician]], heading the newly created [[Australian Bureau of Statistics|Commonwealth Bureau of Census and Statistics]]. In February 1906, he informed Prime Minister [[Alfred Deakin]] that he could not accept the offer due to his obligations to the Premier of New South Wales, [[Joseph Carruthers]]. He later told Deakin that Carruthers had threatened to withdraw his pension entitlements if he accepted the federal position.<ref>{{cite thesis|url=https://openresearch-repository.anu.edu.au/bitstream/1885/112133/4/b12930623_Carment_David_Sulman.pdf|title=Australian liberal: a political biography of Sir Littleton Groom, 1867–1936|first=David|last=Carment|year=1975|publisher=[[Australian National University]]|type=PhD thesis|pages=47–49}}</ref>

In 1912 he represented New South Wales at the [[First International Eugenics Conference]] in London.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://adelphigenetics.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/EUGENICS_IN_AUSTRALIA.pdf|title=Eugenics in Australia: Striving for National Fitness|publisher=The Galton Institute|year=2003|isbn=0950406678|first=Diana|last=Wyndham|pages=119}}</ref>

On 15 December 1914, [[Banjo Paterson]] reports he was in London when he:

{{blockquote|Dropped in for a chat with Sir T.A. Coghlan, our agent-general for New South Wales. As unemotional as a professional billiard player, and as self-reliant as a sea captain, Coghlan has battled his way from a minor civil service job to his present position through sheer ability.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Paterson |first1=A.B. |title=Happy Dispatches |date=1935 |publisher=Angus & Robertson |location=Sydney |page=198 |edition=First}}</ref>}}

It has been said of his work ''Labour and Industry in Australia from the first Settlement in 1788 to the Establishment of the Commonwealth in 1901'':

{{blockquote|This document provided the first great economic history of Australia, covering the period from European settlement to the creation of the Commonwealth … [its] 2449 pages constitute a great, pullulating Victorian panorama in words and numbers that seemingly capture every person, law and landmark … Beyond its use as an encyclopedic reference work, its enduring value lies in its bounty of quantitive data. Much of the latter proved an essential input into estimates of [[national accounts]], other elements remain standing in their own right, with Coghlan's figures for gold production remaining unsuperceded. And posterity has ultimately granted him his famous claim to use his own name as the authority for the statistics he cites.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Ville |first1=Simon |last2=Withers |first2=Glenn |title=The Cambridge Economic History of Australia |date=2015 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Melbourne |isbn=9781107029491 |pages=12, 472 |edition=First}}</ref>}}

Coghlan was serving as Agent-General when he died suddenly at London on 30 April 1926. His funeral was held at [[St Mary's, Cadogan Street]].

In 1897 he married Helen Donnelly (d. 1936),<ref>{{cite news |url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article17324610 |title=LADY COGHLAN. |newspaper=The Sydney Morning Herald |issue=30,606 |location=New South Wales, Australia |date=6 February 1936 |accessdate=17 February 2018 |page=15 |via=National Library of Australia}}</ref> the daughter of [[Denis Donnelly]], who survived him with a son, Austin, and a daughter, Eden. Coghlan left them an estate of the value of [[Australian pound|£]]43,197.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article16332683 |title=LATE SIR TIMOTHY COGHLAN. |newspaper=The Sydney Morning Herald |issue=27,689 |location=New South Wales, Australia |date=2 October 1926 |accessdate=17 February 2018 |page=19 |via=National Library of Australia}}</ref> Coghlan was awarded the [[Imperial Service Order]] (ISO) in 1903, was [[Knight Bachelor|knighted]] in 1914 and created a Knight Commander of the [[Order of St Michael and St George]] (KCMG) in 1918.<ref>{{cite web|title=COGHLAN, Timothy Augustine – Imperial Service Order|url=https://honours.pmc.gov.au/honours/awards/1081704|website=It's an Honour database|publisher=Australian Government|accessdate=16 February 2018|date=29 May 1903|quote=Agent-General for New South Wales in London}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=COGHLAN, Timothy Augustine – Knight Bachelor|url=https://honours.pmc.gov.au/honours/awards/1083272|website=It's an Honour database|publisher=Australian Government|accessdate=16 February 2018|date= 24 February 1914|quote=Agent-General for New South Wales in London}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=COGHLAN, Timothy Augustine – The Order of St Michael and St George- Knights Commander|url=https://honours.pmc.gov.au/honours/awards/1082625|website=It's an Honour database|publisher=Australian Government|accessdate=16 February 2018|date=3 June 1918|quote=Agent-General for New South Wales in London}}</ref>
